$comment: The advice an agent pushes to an employer about its careers site. Every recommendation serves the employer: more of the right applicants, less legal exposure, less wasted work. Tiers: must (legal exposure or excluded from search), should (measured effect on applications), could (differentiation). A recommendation fires when any of its triggers is true: a failed check from check_site.py, or a fact the employer gave. A fact that was never given cannot fire anything; it becomes a question instead. Shared word for word by career-site-builder and careers-site-advisor.

facts.states: US states or DC where the employer posts jobs, as two-letter codes
facts.apply_minutes: how long the application takes on a phone, in minutes
facts.account_required: whether candidates must create an account to apply
facts.resume_required_hourly: whether hourly candidates must upload a resume
facts.jobs_feed: how open jobs reach the careers site: manual or automatic
facts.tracks_source: whether the apply link carries the traffic source into the applicant tracking system
facts.e_verify: whether the employer participates in E-Verify
facts.federal_contractor: whether the employer is a US federal contractor
facts.languages: languages other than English that a meaningful share of candidates prefer
facts.photos: the photography on the site: real, stock or none
facts.job_alerts: whether candidates can sign up to hear when a matching job opens
facts.accessibility_audit: whether a person has audited the site with a keyboard and a screen reader in the last year
facts.eu: whether the employer hires in the European Union

recommendations.title: Show pay as a number on every job
recommendations.why: A dozen states and several cities require a pay range in job postings, and on Indeed postings with an employer-provided salary drew 3.8 times more applications.
recommendations.how: Add pay_min, pay_max and pay_unit to every job in the jobs feed, and show them above the fold and in the structured data.

recommendations.title: Describe benefits on every job page
recommendations.why: California, Maryland, New York and Washington ask for a description of benefits alongside pay in postings, and candidates compare benefits before applying.
recommendations.how: Add a benefits column to the jobs feed, or link each job page to the benefits section; check each state's wording with counsel.

recommendations.title: Link a candidate privacy notice from every page and the application
recommendations.why: California's CCPA covers job applicants and requires a notice at or before collection; a careers site without one is an easy finding in any review.
recommendations.how: Publish an applicant notice (categories, purposes, sources, disclosures, retention, rights) and link it from the footer and the application.

recommendations.title: Say on every page how to ask for an accommodation
recommendations.why: Hiring websites are likely covered by the ADA, and a candidate who cannot use the site needs a working alternative; suits over application portals tend to settle.
recommendations.how: Add a monitored contact for accommodations to the footer and the hiring process section, and decide who answers it and how fast.

recommendations.title: Fix the accessibility failures the check found
recommendations.why: Website accessibility suits rose 27% in 2025 in federal courts alone, and food service is among the most-sued sectors. Each failure here is one a plaintiff's scanner also finds.
recommendations.how: Fix each listed failure: page language, image text alternatives, form labels, visible focus, colour contrast, the dialog.

recommendations.title: Have a person audit the site with a keyboard and a screen reader
recommendations.why: Automated checks find part of the problem. WCAG 2.2 AA is the working benchmark, and the remainder is only found by someone using the site the way a disabled candidate does.
recommendations.how: Commission a manual audit against WCAG 2.2 AA before launch and once a year, and publish an accessibility statement with a way to report a barrier.

recommendations.title: Bring the job markup in line with the search engine's rules
recommendations.why: Job markup that breaks the published guidelines (on a list page, pay in the title, data not visible on the page, missing required fields) can exclude the site's jobs from job search results.
recommendations.how: One JobPosting per job page and none on lists; title field holds the job title only; every marked-up value visible on the page; all required fields present.

recommendations.title: Take filled jobs down the day they close
recommendations.why: Leaving an expired job marked up breaks the search engine's guidelines, and every application to a filled job is a candidate you then have to reject.
recommendations.how: Set a past closing date, return a 404 or 410, or remove the markup, and show similar open jobs on the page instead.

recommendations.title: Display the E-Verify participation and Right to Work notices
recommendations.why: E-Verify participants must clearly display both notices, in English and Spanish, where applicants will see them; online display is allowed.
recommendations.how: Link both notices from the careers site footer and the application.

recommendations.title: Confirm or remove every claim marked for confirmation
recommendations.why: A statistic, benefit or timing on a careers site is a statement the employer makes to every candidate; an unconfirmed one is a promise nobody checked.
recommendations.how: Have the owner of each fact confirm it or remove it before launch; the check report lists every one.

recommendations.title: Remove placeholder text and fix links that go nowhere
recommendations.why: Lorem ipsum, broken links and dead ends tell a candidate the site is not maintained, at the moment they decide whether to apply.
recommendations.how: Replace placeholder text and point every link at a page, a section or the application.

recommendations.title: Let search engines find and index every page
recommendations.why: A missing sitemap, a robots.txt that blocks the site, or pages without a title, description or single main heading keep jobs out of search results.
recommendations.how: Publish a sitemap listing every page, allow crawling, and give each page a title, a description and one h1.

recommendations.title: Put the jobs and the content in the HTML
recommendations.why: In a December 2024 study none of the major AI crawlers rendered JavaScript, so a careers site painted in by JavaScript is invisible when candidates ask an assistant who is hiring nearby.
recommendations.how: Render the job list and every page's text on the server, and link every job page from a plain HTML page.

recommendations.title: Get the application under five minutes on a phone
recommendations.why: Applications under five minutes complete several times more often than those over fifteen, and most still take more than fifteen.
recommendations.how: Cut every question that does not decide eligibility, drop account creation and the resume upload for hourly roles, and time it on a phone.

recommendations.title: Make the site work on a phone, with Search jobs always in reach
recommendations.why: Most frontline candidates search and apply from a phone, and apply rates drop sharply when the mobile experience is poor.
recommendations.how: Add a mobile viewport and keep a Search jobs link in the header of every page.

recommendations.title: Say what happens when a candidate clicks Apply
recommendations.why: When Apply opens a site that looks different, some candidates take it for a scam and leave at the last step.
recommendations.how: Next to the Apply button, say that the application continues on the employer's hiring partner's secure site and roughly how long it takes.

recommendations.title: State the schedule on every job
recommendations.why: Hours decide frontline applications as much as pay; a job without them gets fewer applicants and more early quits.
recommendations.how: One sentence per job: start times, weekends, and how far ahead the schedule is posted.

recommendations.title: Give every job and every location its own page
recommendations.why: Frontline candidates search by town and 'near me'; a page per job carries the markup that search engines list, and a page per location answers the local search.
recommendations.how: Generate a page per open job and per location from the jobs feed, linked from the job search.

recommendations.title: Feed open jobs to the site automatically
recommendations.why: A manually updated careers site drifts: filled jobs stay up, new ones arrive late, and pay goes stale, which costs applicants and breaks the search engine's rules.
recommendations.how: Publish open jobs from the applicant tracking system as a feed the site rebuilds from, at least daily, and use the search engine's indexing API at volume.

recommendations.title: Carry the traffic source into the application
recommendations.why: Without it, recruiting cannot tell which channel produced hires, so spend keeps going to the channels that produce clicks.
recommendations.how: Pass the source parameter from the careers site into the apply link and keep it on the candidate record.

recommendations.title: Help search engines and AI assistants summarise the site
recommendations.why: Organization and FAQ markup, a canonical URL per page and an llms.txt summary make it easier for search engines and assistants to describe the employer correctly.
recommendations.how: Add Organization markup to the home page, FAQPage markup to the FAQ, canonical URLs, and an llms.txt listing pages, jobs and pay.

recommendations.title: Add an equal-opportunity statement
recommendations.why: Expected of many federal contractors under Section 503 and VEVRAA, and a signal candidates look for.
recommendations.how: One sentence in the footer of every page, worded with counsel.

recommendations.title: Replace stock and placeholder imagery with real employees
recommendations.why: Candidates recognise stock photography, and it undoes the specific, honest copy around it.
recommendations.how: Photograph real employees at work with their written consent, and collect short stories in their own words.

recommendations.title: Offer the key pages in the languages candidates prefer
recommendations.why: A translated home page that leads to English-only job pages loses the candidate at the moment that matters.
recommendations.how: Translate the home page, the main career areas, job pages, the FAQ and the hiring process, reviewed by a native speaker.

recommendations.title: Let candidates sign up for a job alert
recommendations.why: A search with no result is a candidate who wanted to work for the employer; an alert keeps them instead of losing them to the next site.
recommendations.how: Offer an alert from every empty search and from the talent community, by text or email, with a one-step stop.

recommendations.title: Replace slogans with specifics
recommendations.why: Phrases candidates have learned to ignore take the space where pay, hours and the actual work should be.
recommendations.how: Swap each flagged phrase for a fact: a timing, a number, what the first week looks like.

recommendations.title: Make the pages lighter
recommendations.why: Heavy pages and third-party scripts are slow on the phone connections many frontline candidates use.
recommendations.how: Compress images, remove unused scripts, and keep each page's HTML, CSS and JavaScript under 500 KB.

recommendations.title: Check the national accessibility and pay-transparency rules in each EU country
recommendations.why: Whether the European Accessibility Act covers an employer's careers site is disputed and some countries go further; the EU pay transparency directive is being transposed into national law.
recommendations.how: Ask counsel in each country where the employer hires which rules apply to its careers site and job postings.
